questions.question: Explain why some amino acids, such as alanine, have more than one genetic code.
questions.answer: The genetic code is degenerate: 64 codons code for only 20 amino acids, so alanine has several codons (GCU, GCC, GCA, GCG).
steps: There are 64 possible codons but only 20 amino acids.
So some amino acids are coded by more than one triplet codon.
Alanine's codons all start GC and differ only in the third base.
This degeneracy means a third-base change is less likely to change the amino acid.

questions.question: Explain the role of the other three genetic codes that do not code for amino acids.
questions.answer: They are stop codons (TAA, TAG, TGA) that signal the end of translation and release the polypeptide.
steps: Three of the 64 codons do not code for any amino acid.
These are the stop codons TAA, TAG and TGA.
They are recognised by release factors at the ribosome.
This stops translation and releases the completed polypeptide chain.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term semi-conservative replication.
questions.answer: Each new DNA molecule contains one original (parent) strand and one newly synthesised strand.
steps: The double helix separates into two template strands.
Each old strand acts as a template for a new complementary strand.
Each new DNA molecule therefore keeps one parental strand.
The other strand in each molecule is newly made, so the process is semi-conservative.

questions.question: Name one enzyme involved in semi-conservative replication.

steps: Semi-conservative replication requires enzymes to unwind and copy DNA.

DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides to the new strand.

questions.question: Explain the importance of semi-conservative replication in producing new cells.
questions.answer: Each new cell gets an accurate, identical copy of the genetic information, so daughter cells are genetically identical.
steps: Before a cell divides, its DNA must be copied.
Semi-conservative replication makes new DNA that is an accurate copy of the original.
Each daughter cell therefore receives the same genetic information.
This keeps the genetic information of the new cells the same as the parent.

questions.question: Name this stage of protein synthesis.
questions.answer: Transcription
steps: The mRNA is made from a DNA template strand.
This happens in the nucleus.
Making mRNA from DNA is called transcription.
Translation is the next stage.

questions.question: Name the enzyme used in this stage of protein synthesis.
questions.answer: RNA polymerase
steps: Transcription needs an enzyme to read the DNA template.
RNA polymerase unwinds DNA and joins complementary ribonucleotides.
It forms phosphodiester bonds 5' to 3'.
So the enzyme is RNA polymerase.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure of an mRNA molecule with that of a tRNA molecule.
questions.answer: Both are single-stranded polynucleotides; mRNA is long and linear with codons, tRNA is short, folded and has an anticodon and amino acid site.
steps: Both are single polynucleotide strands with ribose and bases.
mRNA is long and unfolded, with codons in sequence.
tRNA is short and folded (clover-leaf) with some base pairing.
tRNA has an anticodon and an amino acid attachment site.

questions.question: Describe the structure of collagen.
questions.answer: Collagen has three polypeptide chains wound into a triple helix, with repeating glycine-X-Y sequences, stabilised by hydrogen bonds.
steps: Collagen is a fibrous protein made of three polypeptide chains.
The chains are wound together into a triple helix.
Every third amino acid is glycine, allowing tight packing.
Hydrogen bonds between chains give strength.

questions.question: Calculate the rate of reaction at 30 minutes by drawing a tangent.
questions.answer: Missing: the elastin protease graph is not in the text.

questions.question: Explain how a protease breaks down elastin.
questions.answer: The protease binds elastin at its active site and hydrolyses peptide bonds, splitting the protein into smaller peptides.
steps: Proteases are enzymes that hydrolyse peptide bonds.
The enzyme's active site binds a specific sequence in elastin.
Water is used to break the peptide bonds (hydrolysis).
This splits elastin into smaller peptides and amino acids.

questions.question: Explain how damage to endothelial cells results in the formation of thrombin.
questions.answer: Damaged endothelium exposes underlying collagen and tissue factor, triggering the clotting cascade that converts prothrombin to thrombin.
steps: Healthy endothelial cells prevent clotting.
Damage exposes underlying collagen and tissue factor.
This triggers platelet activation and the clotting cascade.
The cascade converts prothrombin into thrombin.

questions.question: Give one risk of treating patients with anticoagulants.
questions.answer: Excessive bleeding (haemorrhage).
steps: Anticoagulants stop blood from clotting.
This lowers the body's ability to stop bleeding.
So the patient may bleed excessively.
Bleeding (haemorrhage) is the main risk.

questions.question: Which is the minimum number of bases in the gene coding for a 32-amino-acid peptide (A 32, B 33, C 96, D 99)?
steps: Each amino acid is coded by 3 bases: 32 x 3 = 96 bases.
The gene also needs a stop codon (3 bases) to end translation.
Total = 96 + 3 = 99 bases.
Option D is correct.

questions.question: Explain how variegin prevents blood clotting.
questions.answer: Variegin binds to thrombin's active site, blocking it, so thrombin cannot convert fibrinogen into fibrin.
steps: Thrombin needs its active site to act on fibrinogen.
Variegin fits into the active site of thrombin.
It blocks the site (competitive inhibition).
Fibrinogen cannot be converted to fibrin, so no clot forms.

questions.question: Explain how thrombin splits variegin into two molecules.
questions.answer: Thrombin is a protease: its active site binds variegin and hydrolyses a peptide bond, using water, splitting it into two parts.
steps: Thrombin is a protease enzyme.
Its active site binds a specific sequence in variegin.
A peptide bond is broken by hydrolysis, which uses a water molecule.
This splits variegin into two smaller molecules.

questions.question: Which sugar is present in uridine monophosphate?
questions.answer: D - ribose
steps: UMP is a ribonucleotide, found in RNA.
RNA nucleotides contain the sugar ribose.
DNA nucleotides use deoxyribose instead.
Option D (ribose) is correct.

questions.question: Draw a circle around the base in uridine monophosphate.
questions.answer: Missing: the UMP structure diagram is not in the text.

questions.question: Suggest one way cells use uridine monophosphate.
questions.answer: To make RNA (it is a nucleotide monomer used in transcription).
steps: UMP is a nucleotide.
Nucleotides are the building blocks of nucleic acids.
UMP can be phosphorylated to UTP.
UTP is used as a monomer to synthesise RNA.

questions.question: State how OMP decarboxylase increases the rate of the reaction.
questions.answer: It lowers the activation energy by binding the substrate at its active site and straining the bonds.
steps: The enzyme binds orotidine monophosphate at its active site.
This forms an enzyme-substrate complex.
The complex strains bonds and orients the substrate.
So less activation energy is needed, speeding the reaction up.

questions.question: Explain why OMP decarboxylase catalyses this reaction only.
questions.answer: Its active site has a specific shape and charge complementary to only its substrate, so only that reaction is catalysed.
steps: The active site's shape and charge are determined by the enzyme's tertiary structure.
Only the correct substrate can bind (lock and key).
Other molecules do not fit, so they are not converted.
Hence the enzyme is specific to this reaction.

questions.question: Describe the roles of RNA in the synthesis of collagen.
questions.answer: mRNA is transcribed from the collagen gene and carries the code to ribosomes; tRNA brings amino acids; rRNA in ribosomes catalyses peptide bond formation.
steps: Transcription makes mRNA copies of the collagen gene in the nucleus.
mRNA carries the code from the nucleus to ribosomes.
tRNA molecules bring specific amino acids to the ribosome, matched by anticodons.
rRNA forms part of the ribosome and catalyses peptide bond formation.
Together these build the collagen polypeptide chains.

questions.question: Explain how the primary structure of collagen determines its properties.
questions.answer: Its amino acid sequence (repeating glycine-X-Y with proline and hydroxyproline) allows the chains to form a tight triple helix, giving strength and insolubility.
steps: The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids.
Glycine at every third position lets the three chains pack closely.
Proline and hydroxyproline stabilise the helix.
The triple helix and hydrogen bonds give collagen its strength and insolubility.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term gene.
questions.answer: A sequence of DNA bases that codes for a polypeptide (or functional RNA).
steps: A gene is a length of DNA.
Its base sequence contains the code for one polypeptide or functional RNA.
Genes are found at loci on chromosomes.
A gene therefore determines a characteristic.

questions.question: Describe how the two strands of DNA in a gene are held together.
questions.answer: By hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs (A-T and G-C).
steps: The two DNA strands are antiparallel and complementary.
Bases on opposite strands pair up.
Adenine pairs with thymine by two hydrogen bonds.
Guanine pairs with cytosine by three hydrogen bonds.

questions.question: Explain why each codon must contain at least three bases.
questions.answer: Four bases make only 16 combinations (not enough for 20 amino acids), whereas three bases give 64 combinations.
steps: There are 20 different amino acids to code for.
A doublet (two bases from four types) gives 4 x 4 = 16 combinations.
16 is fewer than 20, so it is not enough.
A triplet gives 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 combinations, which is enough.

questions.question: Determine the probability that a child of a colour-blind father and a heterozygous mother is colour blind.
steps: Father: X(c)Y (colour blind). Mother: X(N)X(c) (carrier).
Gametes: father X(c) or Y; mother X(N) or X(c).
Offspring: X(N)Y, X(c)Y, X(N)X(c), X(c)X(c), each 1/4.
Colour blind children are X(c)Y and X(c)X(c), so probability = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.

questions.question: Explain why amylase is able to break only 1-4 glycosidic bonds.
questions.answer: Its active site is shaped to fit the 1-4 linkage of the glucose chain, so it only binds and hydrolyses that bond type.
steps: Enzymes have an active site with a specific shape.
Amylase's active site fits the alpha 1-4 glycosidic linkage.
The 1-6 linkage at branch points has a different shape and does not fit.
So amylase only hydrolyses 1-4 bonds.

questions.question: Suggest how disaccharides and oligosaccharides are broken down in the small intestine, giving reasons.
questions.answer: Specific enzymes on the small intestine lining (e.g. maltase, sucrase, lactase) hydrolyse each disaccharide and oligosaccharide, because each enzyme's active site is specific to one glycosidic bond.
steps: Disaccharides and oligosaccharides are hydrolysed by enzymes on the intestinal wall.
Each disaccharidase (maltase, sucrase, lactase) fits a specific disaccharide.
Oligosaccharides are broken down by enzymes that remove glucose units from the end of the chain.
Specificity of the active site is the reason different enzymes are needed.

questions.question: Explain why glucose cannot diffuse into the bloodstream without membrane transport proteins.
questions.answer: Glucose is a large polar molecule that cannot pass through the hydrophobic phospholipid bilayer of the cell membrane.
steps: Glucose is polar and hydrophilic.
The inner part of the membrane is hydrophobic.
Polar molecules cannot dissolve through the phospholipid bilayer.
A transport protein provides a channel or carrier for glucose.

questions.question: Explain the dipole nature of water.
questions.answer: Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so it pulls shared electrons, giving oxygen a partial negative charge and each hydrogen a partial positive charge.
steps: Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen.
Shared electrons in O-H bonds are pulled towards oxygen.
Oxygen becomes slightly negative and hydrogen slightly positive.
The bent shape means the charges do not cancel, so water is a dipole.

questions.question: Name the current model for the structure of the cell membrane.
questions.answer: The fluid mosaic model
steps: The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer.
Proteins are embedded in or on it.
The components move laterally, so it is fluid.
This is the fluid mosaic model.

questions.question: Describe the arrangement of phospholipids in the cell membrane.
questions.answer: Phospholipids form a bilayer with hydrophilic heads facing outwards to water and hydrophobic tails facing inwards, away from water.
steps: Phospholipids have a hydrophilic phosphate head and hydrophobic fatty acid tails.
In water they form a double layer (bilayer).
The heads face outwards to the aqueous environment on each side.
The tails face inwards and are sheltered from water.

questions.question: Describe the structure of an mRNA molecule.
questions.answer: A single-stranded chain of ribonucleotides (ribose, phosphate and bases A, U, G, C) joined by phosphodiester bonds.
steps: mRNA is a single polynucleotide strand.
Each nucleotide contains ribose, a phosphate and a base (A, U, G or C).
Nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester bonds.
It is linear and carries codons.

questions.question: Explain the arrangement of phospholipids in a lipid nanoparticle that carries mRNA to tissues.
questions.answer: Phospholipids form a sphere with hydrophilic heads facing the watery outside and hydrophobic tails facing inwards, enclosing the mRNA in a protected core.
steps: The nanoparticle is in an aqueous environment, so heads face outwards.
Tails face inwards, away from water, forming a hydrophobic interior.
The hydrophilic, negatively charged mRNA is held in the aqueous core.
This protects mRNA from enzymes and lets it be carried to tissues.

questions.question: Explain why eating soybeans may reduce the risk of heart disease.
questions.answer: Soybean compounds lower cholesterol and LDL in the blood, which reduces atherosclerosis and the risk of heart disease.

questions.question: Give two ways the primary structure of two proteins could differ.
questions.answer: The types of amino acids and the sequence (order) of amino acids can differ, and so can the number of amino acids.
steps: Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids in a chain.
Two proteins can contain different amino acids.
They can also have the same amino acids in a different order.
Either the type, order or number of amino acids gives a valid answer.

questions.question: Explain why the scientists used digested soybeans to make the extract.
questions.answer: Digestion produces the peptides that are absorbed in the gut, so the extract mimics what would reach the liver.
steps: In the human gut, soybean proteins are digested into peptides first.
The peptides, not whole proteins, are what enters the body.
Using digested soybean copies this.
So the results reflect the effect of real absorbed products.

questions.question: Suggest why the soybean flour was incubated with different enzymes in steps 2 and 3.
questions.answer: Different enzymes act at different peptide bonds, copying digestion in the stomach and then the small intestine.
steps: Each protease has a different specificity.
The stomach and small intestine use different enzymes.
Using them in sequence copies the digestive process.
So the soybean protein is fully broken into peptides.

questions.question: Explain why the soybean flour and enzymes were incubated at 37 C for 2 hours.
questions.answer: 37 C is body temperature, the optimum for human digestive enzymes, so they work at their fastest without denaturing.
steps: Human digestive enzymes work best at body temperature.
37 C is the optimum temperature for these enzymes.
This copies conditions in the human gut.
Two hours allows the digestion to proceed to completion.

questions.question: Explain why eating soybeans may reduce blood cholesterol, using the graph of HMGCR activity.
questions.answer: Missing: the graph of HMGCR activity and cholesterol synthesis is not in the text.

questions.question: Describe the role of RNA polymerase in protein synthesis.
questions.answer: RNA polymerase unwinds the DNA and joins complementary ribonucleotides to form mRNA using the template strand.
steps: RNA polymerase binds to the gene's promoter region.
It unwinds the DNA double helix.
It reads the template strand and joins complementary ribonucleotides.
It forms phosphodiester bonds, producing mRNA 5' to 3'.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure of the start and stop codons and how they work.
questions.answer: Both are triplet codons; the start codon AUG codes for methionine and starts translation, while stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) do not code for an amino acid and end it.
steps: Both are triplet (three-base) codons on mRNA.
The start codon AUG codes for methionine and initiates translation.
Stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA do not code for amino acids.
Stop codons are recognised by release factors, which end translation.

questions.question: Describe the roles of ribosomes in protein synthesis.
questions.answer: Ribosomes bind mRNA and tRNA, bringing amino acids together, and rRNA catalyses the formation of peptide bonds.
steps: Ribosomes provide the site for translation.
They hold the mRNA and align tRNAs with their codons.
The ribosome's rRNA catalyses peptide bond formation.
It moves along the mRNA, linking amino acids into a polypeptide.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the genetic code being a triplet code.
questions.answer: Each amino acid is coded for by a sequence of three bases (a codon).
steps: Each codon is made of three consecutive bases.
One codon codes for one amino acid.
For example, GCC codes for alanine.
So the code is read in triplets.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the genetic code being non-overlapping.
questions.answer: Each base belongs to only one codon, so consecutive codons do not share bases.
steps: The code is read in consecutive, separate triplets.
A base in one codon is not used again in the next codon.
This means the reading frame is fixed.
So each base has one specific role in the code.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the genetic code being degenerate.
questions.answer: More than one codon codes for the same amino acid.
steps: There are 64 codons but only 20 amino acids.
So some amino acids have more than one codon.
For example, several codons code for alanine.
Changes in the third base may therefore not change the amino acid.

questions.answer: Missing: the graph of cholesterol and CHD death rate is not in the text.

questions.question: Give two side effects of taking statins.
questions.answer: Muscle pain (myopathy) and liver damage.
steps: Statins lower cholesterol synthesis in the liver.
A known side effect is muscle pain or weakness (myopathy).
Another side effect is raised liver enzymes or liver damage.
Muscle pain and liver damage are the answers.

questions.question: Explain how an increase in LDL receptors helps reduce blood cholesterol levels.
questions.answer: More LDL receptors means more LDL is endocytosed by liver cells, removing cholesterol from the blood.
steps: LDL receptors on liver cells bind LDL particles in the blood.
More receptors means more LDL is bound.
The LDL is taken into liver cells by endocytosis.
So less cholesterol remains in the blood.

questions.question: Calculate the UK population, given about 270 000 people with FH, affecting 1 in 250 people.
steps: Population = number with FH / fraction affected.
In standard form: 6.75 x 10^7.

questions.question: Suggest why statins are less effective in people homozygous for FH.
questions.answer: Homozygous people have little or no functional LDL receptor, and statins work by increasing these receptors.
steps: Statins act by increasing the number of LDL receptors on liver cells.
Homozygous people have two mutant copies of the LDL receptor gene.
They produce little or no functional receptor.
So statins have little effect.

questions.question: Suggest how an antisense strand of DNA from the apo B gene would reduce apo B protein levels.
questions.answer: It binds complementarily to the apo B mRNA, blocking translation or causing the mRNA to be degraded.
steps: The antisense strand is complementary to the apo B mRNA.
It binds to the mRNA by complementary base pairing.
This blocks the ribosome from translating it or marks it for degradation.
Less apo B protein is therefore made.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term semi-conservative replication.
questions.answer: Each new DNA molecule contains one original strand and one newly synthesised strand.
steps: The original double helix separates into two template strands.
Each template is used to make a new complementary strand.
Each new molecule has one old strand and one new strand.
This is semi-conservative.

questions.question: Describe the role of DNA polymerase in DNA replication.
questions.answer: DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides to the 3' end of the new strand, forming phosphodiester bonds, using the template strand.
steps: DNA polymerase reads each template strand.
It matches complementary free nucleotides to the template bases.
It joins each nucleotide to the 3' end of the growing strand.
This forms phosphodiester bonds.

questions.question: Complete the graphs showing the concentrations and densities of DNA at stages 1, 2 and 3 of the flowchart.
questions.answer: Missing: the flowchart and the graph axes are not in the text.

questions.question: Explain how two identical molecules of DNA are produced.
questions.answer: The double helix is unwound and each strand acts as a template for a new complementary strand, so two identical molecules form.
steps: DNA helicase unwinds the double helix, breaking hydrogen bonds.
Each separated strand acts as a template.
DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides to each template.
Each new molecule has one original and one new strand, so both are identical to the parent.

questions.question: Describe the roles of mRNA and tRNA in protein synthesis.
questions.answer: mRNA carries the codons from the gene to the ribosome; tRNA carries specific amino acids, its anticodon pairing with the codons.
steps: mRNA is transcribed from DNA and carries codons to the ribosome.
tRNA carries the specific amino acid for each codon.
tRNA's anticodon pairs with the mRNA codon.
Amino acids are joined in the order set by the codons.

questions.question: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using a Voronoi diagram to show the proportions of molecules in a bacterial cell.
questions.answer: Advantage: it shows the relative proportions clearly by area. Disadvantage: the shapes have no meaning and exact values are hard to read.
steps: Area is proportional to the percentage, so proportions are visible at a glance.
A Voronoi diagram can show many components together.
The shapes carry no meaning, which can confuse the reader.
Exact values are harder to read than in a table or bar chart.

questions.question: Discuss how the appearance of the Voronoi diagram changes as a bacterial cell prepares to divide, in its new daughter cells, and as a daughter cell grows.
questions.answer: Before division the DNA area grows as it is replicated; in each daughter cell the DNA area is halved; during growth the proportions of other molecules rise while DNA's share falls.
steps: Before division, DNA is replicated, so the DNA share of dry mass increases.
Ribosomes and proteins also increase to prepare for division.
After division each daughter cell gets one copy of the DNA, so its DNA area is about half.
As a daughter cell grows, its proteins and RNA increase, so the DNA proportion falls and the diagram changes shape.

questions.question: Explain what determines the properties of an active site.
questions.answer: The primary sequence of amino acids determines the folding (tertiary structure), so the R groups in the active site set its shape and charge.
steps: The amino acid sequence (primary structure) is set by the gene.
This sequence folds into the tertiary structure.
The R groups that line the active site determine its shape and charge.
These properties determine which substrates can bind.

questions.question: Explain why some enzymes cannot function at high temperatures.
questions.answer: High temperature breaks the hydrogen and ionic bonds holding the tertiary structure, so the active site changes shape and the substrate cannot bind.
steps: Enzymes are held in shape by hydrogen, ionic and disulfide bonds.
At high temperature, these bonds break as the molecule vibrates.
The tertiary structure changes, so the active site changes shape.
The substrate no longer fits, and the enzyme is denatured.

questions.question: Suggest why changing the bonding could enable enzymes to work at higher temperatures.
questions.answer: Extra or stronger bonds (e.g. disulfide bonds) need more energy to break, so the tertiary structure and active site stay intact at higher temperature.
steps: Heat breaks bonds that hold the tertiary structure.
Stronger or additional bonds need more energy to break.
So the protein keeps its folded shape at higher temperatures.
The active site therefore stays the correct shape to work.

questions.question: Suggest why changing the bonding could affect the binding of the plastics to the active site.
questions.answer: Changing bonds can alter the shape or charge of the active site, so the plastic no longer fits or binds as well.
steps: The active site's shape and charge determine substrate binding.
Changing the bonding changes the folding.
This alters the shape and charge of the active site.
So the plastic may bind less well, or bind differently.

questions.question: Suggest how a larger active site could increase the rate of breakdown of plastic.
questions.answer: A larger active site can bind more plastic molecules at once, forming more enzyme-substrate complexes per second.
steps: A larger active site has room for more or larger substrate molecules.
More plastic molecules can bind at the same time.
More enzyme-substrate complexes form per unit time.
So more plastic is broken down per second.

questions.question: Suggest why an enzyme with a larger active site may be less active.
questions.answer: A larger, less precisely shaped active site may bind the substrate less tightly or less specifically, reducing the rate.
steps: Enzymes depend on a close, specific fit with the substrate.
A larger active site may hold the substrate less tightly.
Poor fit reduces the number of effective enzyme-substrate complexes.
So the rate of reaction may fall.

questions.question: Explain why linking enzyme 1 to enzyme 2 will speed up the breakdown of plastic.
questions.answer: Enzyme 2 is held next to enzyme 1, so the short chains made by enzyme 1 pass straight to enzyme 2 and are broken into monomers quickly.
steps: Enzyme 1 produces short chains from plastic.
Enzyme 2 is linked close to enzyme 1.
The short chains are passed directly to enzyme 2.
They are broken into monomers quickly, so the overall breakdown is faster.
